section_summary: This section begins with U.S. consular reporting on Japan’s government-sponsored campaign for domestic products, the deepening economic depression, unemployment, silk-market collapse, and rural relief measures. It then transmits a British Department of Overseas Trade handbook on Japanese economic conditions through June 1930. The handbook’s opening chapters survey travel and commercial conditions, the restoration of the gold standard, deflation and government retrenchment, foreign trade, and the silk, artificial-silk, cotton, porcelain, sugar, and flour-milling industries.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 47: Campaign for “Homemade Goods” and the General Economic Condition
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on Japan’s government-sponsored domestic-products campaign and the worsening national economic depression.
subfiles.summary: Garrels describes the nationwide effort to encourage Japanese-made goods, while noting Mayor Ariyoshi’s objection that an anti-import tone conflicted with Japan’s promotion of foreign tourism. He considers American investment in Japan unlikely to be endangered but expects Japan’s industrialization steadily to displace ordinary foreign manufactures. The despatch then reviews deflation, rationalization, falling silk and cocoon prices, rural distress, unemployment, political criticism of government policy, and proposed cuts in ministerial expenditure.

subfiles.title: Postscript to Despatch No. 47 concerning Toshihiko Taketomi’s address
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Introduces an address intended to dispel fears that Japan’s domestic-goods campaign constituted a boycott of foreign products.
subfiles.summary: Postscript to Despatch 47: Garrels sends an excerpt of Toshihiko Taketomi's address to Kobe consuls, in which he denied restrictions beyond the tariff and expressed goodwill.

subfiles.title: “Boycott on Foreign Products Is Not Aim of Home Goods Drive”
subfiles.from: The Japan Times; address by Toshihiko Taketomi
subfiles.about: Publishes Taketomi’s explanation of the aims and limits of Japan’s campaign to promote domestic products.
subfiles.summary: Taketomi presents the home goods campaign as a response to depression, not a boycott, says consumers cannot be compelled to buy inferior goods, warns of failed patriotic campaigns abroad, and stresses goodwill.

subfiles.title: Japanese Governmental Aid: Rural Economic Depression
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes a government loan program intended to relieve acute depression and unemployment in Japan’s agricultural and fishing districts.
subfiles.summary: Rural depression report: falling farm prices and returning urban unemployed prompted a cabinet-approved $35 million from postal savings for agricultural and fishing projects, with loan terms and employment estimates.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1254 transmitting “Economic Conditions in Japan”
subfiles.from: Raymond E. Cox, First Secretary of Embassy, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: Transmits copies of a British Department of Overseas Trade handbook on economic conditions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: London Embassy Despatch 1254 sends three copies of the handbook Economic Conditions in Japan, one for the Tokyo Embassy.

subfiles.title: Economic Conditions in Japan to 30th June, 1930
subfiles.doc_type: published commercial handbook and economic report
subfiles.from: G. B. Sansom and H. A. Macrae
subfiles.to: Department of Overseas Trade and commercial readers
subfiles.about: Presents British commercial guidance and a detailed assessment of Japan’s economy and principal export industries through June 1930.
subfiles.summary: After advertisements, publication information, commercial-service guidance, summary statistics, and travel advice, the report analyzes restoration of the gold standard, deflation, retrenchment, unemployment, falling prices, gold movements, public finance, and the worldwide causes of Japan’s depression. It describes Japan’s trade dependence on the United States and Asian markets and examines the crisis in raw silk, unsuccessful stabilization schemes, silk textiles, artificial silk, and the rapid expansion and rationalization of cotton manufacturing. Subsequent pages detail cotton exports, tariffs, wage reductions, new market initiatives, manufactured cotton articles, porcelain, sugar refining, and the opening of a discussion of flour milling and wheat imports.
